Full disclosure, this story is not technically mine. I'm telling it in the manner in which it was relayed to me. Curiously, parts of the story match my own experience - but that's not important enough to make the distinction.

We Buddhists sometimes go to a monastery to seek refuge. What this means, for us, is that we go to learn. We aren't all able to be monks and may not want to be monks. It's a time of solitude, tranquility, and (if you want it) learning. Some Buddhists go and maintain a vow of silence during their trip - and simply listen and observe. Some may see few other people and seek whatever it is they seek.

This story is from an episode of this. As I mentioned above, this isn't my story. It's confusing, because it was told to me while I was on refuge and the story is about a monk who was a layperson and also was once on refuge. The story is a familiar one, to Buddhists at least. Sure, it varies in the telling - but the principles are much the same. So, from here on out, this isn't technically my story - but is me recounting a story that someone told me. I will write it as I heard it.

Once, I was here at this same monastery and seeking refuge much like you. I worked a regular job, had family and friends, and had what folks would call a pretty good life. I wasn't really comfortable. I wasn't really happy. I didn't feel like I was progressing. I wanted enlightenment and I'd worked really hard to find it. Taking some vacation time, I came to this same monastery and sat much where you sit.

Sitting for a while in meditation didn't help. The flies were too noisy. The wind was too cold. The bustle of the people was too distracting.

Seeing my chance, I went for a walk with one of the venerable. [Note: This is a monk, and may be female. Though, often monks are, in western tongue, called nuns - not to be mistaken for the nuns you see in Christianity.] As we walked, I spoke about my troubles. I spoke about the concerns I had at home. I spoke about how I was never happy with my wife, I was unhappy with my job, and about how I should have no reason to be - but there were all these little stressful things that added up. I spoke about the stresses, things that he probably wouldn't understand. He didn't have a cell phone, wans't on call, didn't have email, and probably didn't have a license so never actually had any car troubles.

We walked and he listened patiently.

Stopping for a moment at a turn in the path, he said simply, "Do you see that rock over there?" I indicated that I did. He instructed me to pick it up, and so I did.

Rock in-hand, we resumed our journey more or less in silence. The rock was uncomfortable and I labored to carry it. I was without much breath to speak.

We continued on this way for some time. Him in silence and me with labored breath as I carried the rock.

Finally, I could take no more and stopped. He told me that I should put the rock down and I was happy to oblige.

Catching my breath, I stood where we'd stopped alongside a stream. I marveled a bit at the calmness of the moment. When he spoke, he said, "Is the rock still heavy?"

I had to admit that it was not. I confessed, I didn't understand. He said to me, "The rock is only heavy if you carry it."

Burdens are only heavy if you carry them. If the stone is heavy, let it go.

Our stones are the things we desire. They are the fast cars, money, happiness, love and attention, and all those things. Those are all desires. We can't all be monks and live without desire, but we can choose some of the burdens we carry. From desire comes suffering. We want more, we want bigger, we want to live forever, we want to never get sick, we want to never get old, and we want to never die. We want to be in control, we want to be loved, we want to be given attention. Those are all desires - and, it's the desire for those things that causes suffering. If you don't desire to live forever, death doesn't hold power over you.

Those burdens, they are our causes of suffering. The stone isn't heavy if you don't carry it. Some of those stones make no sense to carry. Sure, we all pick some burdens to shoulder, because we're not monks. Wisdom is knowing what burdens to carry, and which ones to throw away. Or, maybe that's enlightenment? I don't struggle to be happy - I accept being content, and that makes me happy.

I'm not saying lay down and just let everything go, I'm saying let those burdens go that you have no control over. I'm saying when the weight is too great, let it go. The weight of the world is heavy, don't carry it. The fear of death comes from our desires to live forever, to accomplish more, to control everything, to be master of our own destiny. Let it go. Don't carry those burdens. Don't lug those needless stones around with you. When life ends, you don't get to take a pile of useless rocks with you.

Just let it go.

It's not easy - but the answer is easy. How you learn to let it go is your path. No two people can cross the same stream - it's different every time. And, without the struggle, there is no struggle.

The path is mindfulness, by the way. The path is learning to be mindful - mindful of which burdens you pick up and carry, as well as mindful of many things. It's being mindful of how you breathe, it's being mindful of how your words affect others, it's being mindful to be a good person, it's being mindful to be healthy, it's being mindful to be attentive to others. You're not a monk, you're never going to be a monk. You don't need to try to live completely without desire - that's just crazy talk. Only crazy fucking monks do that, and even they have desires 'cause they're humans.

By the way, there's no deity in this. It's compatible with no religion or any religion. Everyone is a Buddhist - they just don't know it. Some are worse Buddhists than others and we're all terrible Buddhists. If you want to be a good Buddhist, the objective is to be mindful and have the Buddha spirit - but that's not important. In fact, Buddhism really doesn't have much to do with the story, except it provides the background.
